General Ordination of the Roman Missal, 114. Inter Missas autem ab aliquibus communitatibus celebratas peculiarem locum obtinet Missa conventualis, quae pars est Officii cotidiani, aut Missa, quae " communitatis ", dicitur. Et quamvis hae Missae nullam specialem formam celebrationis prae se ferant, maxime tamen decet eas cum cantu fieri, praecipue cum plena participatione omnium sodalium communitatis sive religiosorum sive canonicorum. In iis proinde munus suum exerceant singuli iuxta Ordinem vel ministerium receptum. Expedit ideo ut omnes sacerdotes qui pro utilitate pastorali fidelium singulariter celebrare non tenentur, in iis, quantum fieri potest, concelebrent. Omnes insuper ad eam communitatem pertinentes sacerdotes qui officio in bonum pastorale fidelium singulariter celebrandi tenentur, Missam quoque conventualem aut "communitatis" eadem die concelebrare possunt. Praestat enim presbyteros, qui celebrationi eucharisticae intersunt, nisi iusta causa excusentur, munus proprii ordinis de more exercere et proinde uti concelebrantes participare, sacris vestibus indutos.

Chapter 1

Introduction

Article 1: The Importance of Liturgy

1“Every liturgical celebration, because it is an action of Christ the High Priest and of His Body, the Church, is a sacred action surpassing all others; no other action of the Church can equal its efficacy by the same title and to the same degree.”1 This action is so, regarding the Holy Eucharist in which “the common spiritual good of the whole Church is substantially contained… 2 that is Christ Himself.” 3

Article 2: The Priesthood of Christ

2At the liturgy, it is Christ Himself who continues to exercise His eternal Priesthood through those whom, in different ways, He has extended His own priesthood through Baptism, Confirmation and Holy Orders. “The liturgy is considered an exercise of the priestly office of Jesus Christ.” 4 “Through the liturgy Christ, our redeemer and high priest continues the work of our redemption in, with, and through his Church.” 5

Article 3: A Glorified God and Sanctified Men

3In “this great work … God is perfectly glorified and men are sanctified.” 6 Thus “in the Liturgy, the whole public worship is performed by the Mystical Body of Jesus Christ, that is, by the Head and his members”; or, in other words, “the Church is His beloved Bride who calls to her Lord and through Him offers worship to the Eternal Father.” 7

Article 4: The Work of Salvation

4The Saving Work Christ entrusted to His Apostles is performed at the Liturgy “by means of sacrifice and sacraments, around which the liturgical life revolves.”8 It is particularly performed at the Eucharistic Sacrament – Sacrifice. The Eucharist is like “the consummation of the spiritual life and the pinnacle of all the other Sacraments.” 9

Article 5: The Church

5The entire Universal Church offers the Sacrifice of the Mass 10 as She is also offered. 11 Through the Liturgy the Church manifests who She is. The Liturgy then, is the “Church’s Epiphany, since the Liturgy is the Church at prayer.” 12 “In the Liturgy, the Mystery of the Church is distinctively proclaimed, experienced and lived.” 13

6The liturgy is also the action of Christ and of the Church:

- of Christ, because He is the unique and true High Priest (Heb 8:1);

- of the Church, because “in this great work… God is perfectly glorified and men are sanctified. The Church is His beloved Bride who calls to her Lord. Through Him, She offers worship to the Eternal Father.” 14

Article 6: The Blessed Virgin Mary

7Since the liturgy is Christ and the Church’s action, it is therefore also the action of the Most Blessed Virgin Mary. “Mary shares a great intimacy with both Christ and the Church. Because of this intimacy, She can not be separated from Them. She is also united to each, first in what constitutes the very essence of the Liturgy itself, since the Liturgy is the sacramental celebration of Salvation for the glory of God and, second, in the sanctification of man. Mary is present at the memorial, the liturgical action, in the same way that she was with Christ during His Saving Work. 15

Article 7: The Hierarchy

8“Since the Pope has the Peter’s ministry in the Church, he is associated with every celebration of the Eucharist, wherein he is named as the sign and servant of the unity of the universal Church. The bishop of the diocese or jurisdiction is always responsible for the Eucharist, even when another priest presides. The bishop’s name is mentioned to signify his presidency over the particular Church, in the midst of his presbyterium and with the assistance of deacons. The community intercedes also for all ministers who, for it and with it, offer the Eucharistic sacrifice.”undefined 16

Chapter 2

The Purpose of this Directory

Article 1: Objective

9This Directory’s objective is not to present a liturgical theology, or to replace any approved instruction. Rather, its purpose is to mark a ‘style’ of worthy, sober, solemn, with a liturgical rhythm, festive, faithful and creative sacred celebrations. Our aim is not for banal or superficially noisy, nor secularized or unsacred, nor vulgar or childish, nor exaggerated or rigid celebrations. In addition, this Directory aspires to declare the religious and the educational importance of the Sacred Liturgy for our Religious Family 17.

Article 2: A Style

10An essential part of our Charisma is our commitment to highlight a style on our liturgical celebrations in which the Word is incarnated, sacramentally-incarnated. Celebrations which continually emphasize the prevailing presence and action of the Principal Priest, 18 celebrations in which it is perceived that the essential attitude of the secondary priest is an attitude of prayer, typical of someone who knows he is a mere instrument, imperfect and subordinated to the primary cause and its purposes, and celebrations in which all the visible elements help those who are in the presence of the Mystery to realize the splendorous presence of what is Invisible.

11Our liturgical celebrations must be an example: “by the rites, by the spiritual and pastoral tone, and by the due fidelity to the prescriptions and texts of liturgical books, as well as to norms issued by the Holy See and the Episcopal Conferences.” 19

Chapter 3

The Participation

Article 1: The Participation

12The Church vehemently “wishes to guide all the faithful to take part totally, consciously, and actively (and ‘fruitfully’ 20) in the liturgical celebrations.” 21 Total Participation means it should be manifested in the exterior postures: gestures, prayers, and songs, as well as in the interior: a firm will to be united with Christ and His Mystical Body. Conscious participation means to be fully aware of what one is doing and why, not merely ‘to be present’ in a negligent absentminded way. Active participation means everybody should take part: “They must not attend this mystery of faith… like strangers or silent spectators.” 22 It must be cultivated in the acclamations, responses, Psalms, antiphons, gestures, and bodily positions. 23 Fruitful participation is the perfect participation. It is the ‘completion’ of the liturgical participation. The Sacramental Communion constitutes the maximum and most effective way of participating.

13Liturgical renewal “cannot be restricted to the ceremonies, rites, texts, etc. Moreover, active participation does not consist solely of external activity, but, above all, of an internal and spiritual joining in the living and sacred participation of the celebration of the Paschal Mystery of Jesus Christ. 24” 25

14Our Liturgies must be lively and fully experienced by the community: lively, that is to say, vivacious, powerful, effective and radiant, and fully experienced by the community, full of life; an immediate experience of the Eucharistic Jesus. “The liturgy must foment the sense of the sacred and make it radiant. It must be filled with a spirit of reverence and God’s glorification.” 26

Article 2: Sacramental Character and different ways of Participation

15The essential differences, not related to degree, that occur in the liturgical actions reside in the different sacramental characters. In fact, the Sacraments of the New Law are ordered for two aims: to be a remedy against sins and to perfect the soul regarding God’s worship according to the Christian Religion’s rites. However, as the Sacraments destine men to the spiritual service of God’s worship, they seal the Faithful with a certain spiritual character.

16The sacramental character perfects the man in such a way that it makes him “divine and transmitter of the divine.” 27 Saint Thomas adds: “Since divine worship consists of receiving the divine mysteries or transmitting them to another one, a certain power is necessary for each one of these services: active, to transmit; passive, to receive. The character has, of its own, a spiritual power related to the divine rites.” 28

17The sacramental character “is primarily a seal that characterizes something as ordered to a certain aim.” The Christian faithful are destined for two things: “first and principally for the enjoyment of glory… secondly, each of the faithful is deputed to receive or to bestow what is about God’s worship: and this, properly speaking, is the purpose of the sacramental character. Now the whole rite of the Christian religion is derived from Christ's priesthood. Consequently, it is clear that the sacramental character is Christ’s character, to whose priesthood the faithful are configured according the sacramental characters; these are none other than certain participations of Christ's Priesthood, flowing from Christ Himself.” 29

18The sacrament ordered to provide ministers for the divine worship is Holy Orders. “By this sacrament, some men are destined to provide others with the rest of the Sacraments.” 30 The sacrament ordered to provide subjects for divine worship is Baptism. “Through the virtue of this sacrament, man is enabled to receive the rest of the Church’s sacraments …. In a certain way, it is the same for Confirmation….” 31

19For this reason it is established in our Constitutions: “This participation in Christ’s Priesthood is the essence of the sacramental character that begins with Baptism, is perfected with Confirmation and achieves its plenitude in Holy Orders.” 32

Chapter 4

Priesthood and Participation

Article 1: Common Priesthood and Participation

20“The baptismal character empowers us to receive the other sacraments. It empowers the lay faithful to act as their own proper ministers in the sacrament of Marriage which is the maximal realization of the common priesthood. How we should nurture our soul with the reality of our Baptism! How we should teach this reality to the Christian lay faithful!” 33

21“The baptismal character enables all the baptized to specially offer the Eucharistic Sacrifice. This grandiose and amazing prerogative should be insistently taught especially to all the members of our Institutes who are not ministerial priests. The baptized participate, though without carrying out the liturgical rite themselves, in the oblation to the Father of the Altar’s Victim in two ways: 1st they offer the Sacrifice by means of the visible priest, since he offers on behalf of all the members when acting in Persona Christi (the Person of Christ) as Head and Shepherd; 2nd they also offer the Sacrifice together with the visible priest when they unite to this Sacrifice their vows of praise, supplication, and atonement.” 34

22First, then, by means of the visible priest, at each Mass that is celebrated, in the offering of the Church, all its members, all the baptized ones, including the shepherds, offer the Sacrifice through the hands of the main priest. This priest, acting in persona Christi, the Head, 35 offers the Sacrifice in the name of all the Christian faithful, as it is read in the anaphora: “Remember, Lord, your people...; 36 accept this offering from your whole family”; 37 and still: “we offer you this sacrifice of praise for ourselves .…” 38 These words clearly show that, by means of the visible priest, all the baptized offer the Sacrifice, men, women, children and the elderly, seculars and consecrated men and women.

23Because of their baptismal character, it is presumed that all the faithful give consent in all the Sacrifices the Church offers. They virtually want these Sacrifices to be offered in their name also, through the visible priest. In addition, they consent to be recipients, as it is proper to them, of the fruits of each Mass that is celebrated anywhere in the world and at every hour. For this reason Pope Innocent III taught: “Not only the priests offer [the Sacrifice], but the faithful also, since what is particularly carried out through the ministry of the priests is also universally carried out through the faithful’s baptismal vows.” 39 For this reason the ministerial priest was chosen publicly to offer the Sacrifice in the name of all.

24Second, along with that offering of the visible priest, the faithful unite their act of praises and vows so that in the same oblation of the Victim and the external rite of the visible priest, they are truly presented and offered to God the Father “as living, holy and pleasing hosts to God.” (Rom 12:1)

25“The character of Confirmation, through the comforting or corroborative grace, enables us to confess our faith in Christ with courage and fortitude and to defend it against its opponents with greater ease and naturalness.” 40

26“The character of Holy Orders configures the ministerial priest with Christ-the-Head, giving him power over the physical and mystical Body of Christ. It allows him to act ‘in persona Christi.’ 41 His main role is in the immolation and oblation of the Sacrifice of the Mass. It is also his office to bless, preside, preach, baptize, to hear confessions, etc. The ministerial priest-members of our Institute should return again and again to that ineffable reality which operated in them to change ontologically through their configuration to Christ-the-Head. No ‘secular spirituality’ should shrink their ‘priestly spirituality’.” 42

Article 2: Ministerial Priesthood and Participation

27Without a doubt, the liturgical celebrations will generally be what the celebrant “wants” and “is”. He must be vigilant that every detail in the celebration is what it should be. He is to celebrate with unction but without affectation, with solemnity but without pomposity, with fidelity, without excepting a sane creativity, with devotion but without false piety, with the conscience that the principal operator is Jesus Christ, the principal Priest, showing Christ transparently, not an opaque membrane obstructing the people’s vision to Christ.

28As blessed Pope John XXIII remarked, Saint John Maria Vianney, the holy Priest of Ars, is an example of this required spirit. Saint John would say, “The reason for the relaxation in many priests’ moral lives is because they do not offer the Sacrifice with attention and piety.” 43

29“He did everything there was to be done to stir up the reverence and love of the faithful for Christ hidden in the Sacrament of the Eucharist and to bring them to be nurtured by Holy Communion. The example of his devotion was ever before them. To be convinced of this, a witness says, it was enough to see him celebrating the Holy Mass or simply doing genuflection when passing in front of the tabernacle.” 44

Chapter 5

Words and Gestures

Article 1: Words and Gestures

30The visible elements have great importance in the liturgy. The pronunciation of the words should be observed with a certain rhythm, neither fast nor slow, neither blaring nor dim in voice, said with expression, without theatricality, with sincerity, clarity, precision, originality, unction. It should evoke in those participating that which God says or hears. We must keep in mind through the pronunciation of the words God becomes present and is made manifest. 45

31The liturgical gestures must be full, not unnecessarily repeated, ordered, human, not like coming from automatons. Gestures are not to be omitted. The quality of our celebrations must be meticulously scrutinized even to the smallest details; neglected, loose, unprepared, hurried, verbose-wordy, anodyne and dull celebrations debilitate the faith of those participating.

32The necessity of remote and proximate preparation for the Holy Mass will never be over-emphasized. In fact, our day should be divided in two: one is for preparation, the other for thanksgiving. There is nothing more important in our Christian life than the Mass. When we celebrate or participate in It, the day is already won. For this reason, in some sacristies, we find that wise warning: “Celebrate this Mass as it would be the first one, the last one, and the only one.” 46

Article 2: Three Examples of Full Gesture

33The first of these full gestures is Concelebration: “Through Concelebration the Sacrifice and the Priesthood’s unities are suitably expressed. Moreover, when the faithful actively participate in it, the unity of the People of God shines extraordinarily. It also signifies and fortifies brotherly bonds among the priests.…” 47 It is preferred that in conventual or ‘communitarian’ Masses all priests concelebrate in It: “It is desirable then, in these cases, that all priests who have no obligation to celebrate individually for the faithful, should concelebrate in these Masses. Moreover, all the priests belonging to a Community, who have the obligation to celebrate individually for the faithful, can concelebrate the same day in the conventual or ‘communitarian’ Mass.” 48 In a special way at the seminaries: “...the Mass must be celebrated by all the Seminary’s community in which each one is to participate according to his rank. For this reason it is fitting that priests who live at the seminary and who have no obligation to celebrate elsewhere by pastoral office, concelebrate at the communitarian Mass. Deacons, acolytes and readers are to exercise their own functions.” 49

34A second example of full gesture is the Communion under both species, when it is permitted, since “it acquires a bountiful form as a sign… the sign of the Eucharistic banquet is more perfectly shown and that Will, which ratifies the New and eternal Covenant in the Blood of Christ and the bond between the Eucharistic and the eschatological banquet in the Kingdom of the Father (cfr. Mat 26:27-29), is more clearly expressed.” 50 “Communion under both species, which if considered as a sign, presents a more bountiful form and is recommended at the seminary.” 51

35A third example of full gestures is receiving Communion with hosts consecrated at the same Mass: “Let it be offered at the altar as much holocaust as sufficient for the people.…”52 “...At Mass, the priest gives (in Communion) part of the same Victim offered by himself... and satisfies the piety and the right petition of those who, attending the Mass, ask to be admitted at the participation of the same Sacrifice….”53 “Worthy of praise are those who, being present at the Sacrifice, receive hosts consecrated in It….”54 “It is specially recommended the most perfect form of participation at Holy Mass, which consists of receiving, the faithful, after the priest’s personal communion, the Body of the Lord from the same Sacrifice.”55 “It should be procured that the faithful receive hosts consecrated at the same Mass that, through this sign, Communion as a participation at the same celebrated Sacrifice be more perfectly shown.”56

Article 3: Song and Music

36“The liturgical action acquires a nobler form when celebrated with song... Prayer adopts then, a more penetrating expression.”57 Through singing “the mystery of the Liturgy is more clearly manifest.”58

37Song is a “necessary or integral part of the solemn liturgy.”59 Even more “song is a sign of euphoria, joy, happiness of the heart. From here Saint Agustin rightly affirms: “Singing is proper to the lover.””60 For that reason the one who loves not, who is absorbed in himself, does not sing. Song, then, is not merely ornamentation as something external to prayer.

38The great values of singing in the liturgy are:

1) Song expresses and shapes inner attitudes: song expresses ideas, feelings, attitudes, and desires. It is a universal language -together with the word, the gesture, the movement, and the dance-. It is a sign of expression of sorrow, happiness, triumph, protest. It often reaches where the single word does not.

It also shapes the inner attitude. It brings to life the inner feelings and feeds them. It moves us and, somehow, is an incarnation of our inner attitudes. It makes prayer more complete. It encompasses the whole of the person in prayer since it touches his feelings and esthetical capacity.

392) Song creates Community. “Through the union of voices a more total union of hearts is made possible.”61 In a fuller and perfect way it manifests “the communitarian nature of the Christian worship.”62

Singing creates a harmonious atmosphere and is a sign of solidarity and communion. Singing helps to get out of ourselves, surpassing merely personal perspectives and so be incorporated into the communitarian perspectives.

We are a community, and singing is one of its most prevalent signs and cause of our common sensitivity.

The reluctance of some for singing is often due to a false individualism, selfishness, since singing with others helps us leave ourselves and adhere to the communitarian expression in a unique celebration.

403) Singing brings out a festive celebration:

- it shapes a more festive or solemn atmosphere

- it expresses prayer with much gentleness

- it fosters unity

- it enriches the sacred rites with a greater solemnity63

- it is the clearest prefiguring of the joy of the heavenly liturgy

41Solemnity and festivity are manifested in the community that takes part in singing. When the celebration is in common and sung, then that is the real festival: “there is nothing more festive and pleasing... than a whole assembly who expresses its faith and piety through singing.”64

42For that reason it is proposed to us “to sing with joy the liturgy of the Hours.”65 “Blessed are the people who know the festal shout.”66

434) Singing has a “ministerial function,”67 the result of singing in the liturgy, is not owed to its own musical nature, nor to its being received in Tradition, nor to its pedagogical value. Rather, it comes from the celebration itself, considered as a liturgical rite with its proper identity and laws, and from the celebrant community.

44Singing must lead this particular community to celebrate in unity. For this reason singing is not ‘independent’ but ‘ministerially’ serves the Rite celebrated by the gathered community. This is the reason why each song’s exigencies must be respected if it is an acclamation, a processional song, a song for meditation, litanic response, hymn of glory, etc.

45“The more intimately linked to the liturgical action a song is, the holier it becomes.”68

465) Singing is like a sacrament; at the celebration, the song and the music are certain efficacious signs of the inner event.

47It is the “incarnation” of a mystery taking place at deeper levels: a God who speaks and creates His gift, and a Community who responds with faith, praise and pleas. Singing is one of the effective signs of this “encounter”. Even more than this, it is an efficacious sign of the praise of all humanity and the cosmos: “United with them, and in the name of every creature under heaven, we too praise your glory as we sing….”69

48A singing Community is also sign of Christ’s presence: “Who is present when the Church pleads and sings psalms”70. It is ‘the bride’s voice’ united to the Bridegroom in the sacrificium laudis (sacrifice of praise).

Chapter 6

Other Liturgical Celebrations

Article 1: Liturgy of the Hours

49It is also necessary to recognize the importance of the pious and devout prayer of the Liturgy of the Hours, previously known as the Divine Office or Breviary. A helpful document for understanding its importance is the “Laudis Canticum.”71 It is also necessary to recognize its importance as a preparation and prolongation of the Holy Mass.72

50The main Hours of the Divine Office ordinarily are to be prayed in community.73

Article 2: Penance celebrations

51In our communities, as far as possible, penance celebrations should take place every week, on a fixed day, according to the Ritual of Penance.74

Article 3: The Liturgical Seasons

52The different liturgical seasons are to be celebrated as rightfully due. In a special way, the celebration of the Octave of Easter as a Great Sunday is an ongoing tradition among us. Solemnities scheduled in the Canonical Right Code75 and every Apostle’s Feast are also to be observed.

Article 4: Other Cares

53Maximum attention must be given concerning reverential care for tidiness in regards to the altar and the celebrant’s trousseau. The ornaments are to be worthy and beautiful. The chalice cup should preferably be made of silver; the altar, made of stone; the celebrant and reader’s pulpits are to be fixed. All material is to be ‘noble,’ including the images.76 Let’s have no concern about spending money for the splendor of the worship. Philip II was reproached for his bedroom’s floor at the Escorial, made of brick; and he answered: “A palace for God, a hut for the king.”

54Much attention is to be paid concerning the different liturgical ministries: the ministry of hosting (perhaps it would be more biblically correct to call it ‘hospitality’), the guide, the offering collectors, the servers or acolytes, the readers.… Attention should be paid, in a very special way, to the people guiding the sacred music and songs, whether it be a polyphonic choir or Gregorian, the psalmist or the soloist.

Chapter 7

Permanent Formation

55Taking into consideration all that has been stated here, it is essential to include into our permanent formation’s programs, time for the study of the Liturgy. Every year, the following documents should be read and/or carefully reviewed:

- A good book on the Eucharist, a review on the General Introduction for the Roman Missal, a review on the Primary Notes to the different sacraments’ rituals77 and to the Lectionary,78 the Norms for the liturgical year and the universal Calendar,79 the norms for the Liturgy of the Hours,80 and the norms for the Sacramentals,81 etc.

It is even advisable, considering the advancements in modern technology, to record on video some of our Masses, and so have the advantage of watching ourselves in the way people see us. Perhaps we would be surprised to see certain ‘tics’ or ‘faults’ in our gestures, words, or attitudes, and the lack of observance of norms: in the exterior and in the spirit with which they are to be observed. We should probably answer to blessed John XXIII’s invitation: “With fatherly affection we ask our dear priests to examine from time to time the way they celebrate the divine mysteries.…”82 It is also useful to attend or to see a video of Masses presided by other priests, specially by Our Holy Father the Pope, since He is a living example of how the liturgy should be celebrated... Every liturgy should be, as far as possible, cathedraly.

Chapter 8

Diverse Rites and Cultures

Article 1: All the Rites

56Everyone who has a genuine catholic soul should learn to appreciate the diversity of liturgical rites that show the catholicity of the Church, its sane pluriformity, the wonderful richness of its more pure traditions. It is necessary to learn how to breathe using both lungs: “one can not breathe like a Christian, or better said as a Catholic, with a single lung; it is necessary to have two lungs, that is to say, the Eastern and the Western.”83 It is also important to know and help, as far as possible, those Eastern and Western liturgical traditions that are in most need of it. For that reason, we already have an Eastern branch in our Congregation.

Article 2: Liturgy and Cultures

57Since we want to reach every man with the Gospel, we want to inculturate and adapt the liturgy if it is required. “The celebration of the liturgy must correspond to the mind set and the culture of the different people.84 In order to make the Mystery of Christ ‘known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of the faith’ (Rom. 16, 26), this Mystery should be announced and lived in all the cultures; and these are not abolished but rescued by It.85”86

58The inculturation, understood as “the incarnation of the Gospel in the different regional cultures and at the same time the introduction of these cultures into the life of the Church,”87 has its own place in the Cult as in other fields of the Church’s life.88 A liturgy taking root in diverse cultures “constitutes one of the aspects of the Gospel’s inculturation, that which demands a true integration of the permanent values of a culture at the life of faith of each nation, rather than the transient ones. This work must, then, be inseparably united to a vast action and a harmonized pastoral that considers all the aspects of the human condition.”89

59For the inculturation and adaptation of the liturgy we are to consider the principles exposed by the Church: “At the liturgy, above all the sacramental, there is an immutable part of a divine institution for which the Church is only its guardian. There are also parts susceptible to change, of which the Church has the power, and sometimes the duty, to adapt to the cultures of the recently evangelized nations.90”91

60Other considerations in our study and inculturation of the Roman rite are the proper AIM of Inculturation, the Substantial UNITY of the Roman rite, and the Competent AUTHORITY.92

a) “The aim that must guide the inculturation of the Roman rite is the same that the Second Vatican Council has set as a foundation for the general restoration of the liturgy: to order the texts and the rites in such a way that they express, with more clarity, the holy things they signify, and as far as possible, that the Christian people may easily understand them and so participate in these rites through a full, active, and communitarian celebration.” 93

b) “…The process of inculturation will be implemented in keeping with the substantial unity of the Roman rite. This unity is actually expressed in the approved liturgical books published under the authority of the Holy Father and books sanctioned by the Episcopal Conferences for their respective countries and confirmed by the Holy See. Our study of the inculturation should not search for the inclusion of families of new rites; since an adaptation, due to the necessities of a certain culture, means to have these new adaptations as part of the Roman rite also, not out of it.” 94

c) …The adaptations of the Roman rite, also considering inculturation, depends solely upon the authority of the Church. This authority resides in the Holy See and is exercised through the Congregation for the Divine Worship and the discipline of the sacraments, within the limits established by the Canon Law, the Episcopal Conferences, and the diocesan bishop.… The inculturation, therefore, is not left to the personal initiative of the celebrant or the common initiative of the Christian assembly.”95

Conclusion

61All the efforts we make to improve our liturgies will always be minuscule, considering the greatness of the Mystery which we celebrate, the greatness of the fruits we receive, and the produced effects. After praying for what he needed, at the celebration of the Holy Mass, Saint Leopold Mandic would respectfully say: “Now refuse to answer my prayers if you are able to, Oh Lord.”96
